analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from giving part-time workers worse pay, schedules, leave, and retirement benefits than full-timers.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral in the House and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, without a hearing, vote, or action in any of its five committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make part-time employees eligible for family and medical leave after 12 months on the job, no matter how few hours they work, and let long-term part-timers join 401(k) plans within 24 months. It would also bar employers from paying part-timers less or treating them worse than full-timers doing the same work, require large employers to offer extra hours to current employees before hiring new ones, and give workers the right to sue over violations. It was referred to five House committees in February 2020 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temp workers — retail, restaurant, warehouse, and care workers who often get no paid leave, no 401(k), fewer benefits, and unpredictable schedules — would gain access to family and medical leave, workplace retirement plans, equal pay and benefits for equal work, and first claim on extra hours at their own job.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the requirement that employees work a minimum number of hours in the previous 12 months before qualifying for family and medical leave, so part-timers become eligible after 12 months of employment [S2].

It caps any service requirement for 401(k) participation at two consecutive 12-month periods of at least 500 hours for part-timers age 21 and over, and lets the Labor Department fine employers $10,000 per year per worker for plans that refuse to comply [S2][S3].

It prohibits employers from setting worse pay, notice of work hours, paid time off, or promotion opportunities for part-timers doing substantially equal work, with a private right of action, double (liquidated) damages, and attorney's fees for workers who sue [S2][S3].

It requires employers to record each worker's desired weekly hours and to offer available extra hours to existing employees before hiring new workers, staffing agencies, or contractors, and to pay existing employees for hours worked by those new hires when the employee was available [S3].
It prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who exercise these rights, and requires employers to keep three years of compliance records that employees can inspect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — companies with more than 500 employees (and chains or franchises counted together) — would bear the cost of equalizing pay and benefits, expanding leave and 401(k) eligibility, building scheduling systems that offer hours to current staff first, and keeping compliance records. Smaller employers with 15 or fewer employees are exempt from the fair-treatment rules [S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring pay, leave, and 401(k) parity for part-timers could raise labor costs sharply for large retail, restaurant, and franchise employers, and some may respond by converting part-time jobs to fewer full-time positions or hiring outside contractors to avoid the coverage rules [S3].

The offer-of-hours rule would force employers to build systems to track each employee's stated availability and pay existing workers for hours taken by new hires, an administrative burden that goes beyond current wage-and-hour law [S3].
Even supporters would acknowledge the bill applies primarily to very large employers, so most part-time workers at small businesses would see no change [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real gap: millions of part-time workers are excluded from family leave and 401(k) plans and are often paid less for the same work. The costs fall on large employers, in higher benefit expenses and new scheduling systems; the risk is reduced part-time hiring or more contracting out. As written, the rules apply only to employers above 500 employees, which limits both the benefit and the disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced and two of its provisions were referred to subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on February 27, 2020, joined by Representatives DeLauro, Porter, and Pressley [S1][S3].

It was referred to the Education and Labor, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees; portions went to the Worker and Family Support and Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties subcommittees [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill received no further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers that would have had to equalize pay, benefits, and leave for part-timers are better off; part-time workers gained nothing, and the narrower protections they have under existing law remained unchanged.

for.name: Reps. Rosa DeLauro, Katie Porter, and Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had four Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no one ever had to vote yes or no on the record.

industries.industry: Large employers (retail, restaurant, warehouse, and franchise chains)
industries.note: The bill's fair-treatment rules cover employers with more than 500 employees, counting franchises and chains in the aggregate. These employers would have to pay part-timers the same as full-timers for equal work, extend leave and 401(k) eligibility, and offer current staff extra hours before hiring, which is why the bill matters mostly as a cost avoided for this group.

The bill bars large employers from using temp agencies or contractors to fill hours that existing part-time employees have said they want. It also covers joint-employer arrangements, pulling agency workers into the protections.

Requiring 401(k) and 403(b) plans to admit long-term part-time workers would add millions of small-balance participants to employer plans, modestly expanding the industry's client base along with workers' savings.
